• ICU
  • DEPARTMENT MANUAL
  • INTRODUCTION
    • Critical care unit:
      • It is a specially staffed and equipped hospital ward dedicated to the management of patients with life-threatening illnesses, injuries or complications.
      • At HOSPITAL, We have three types of critical care units:
        • ICU: For multi system disease patients
      • All three critical care units are managed by qualified & trained nursing staff & doctors & equipped with lifesaving equipment’s like ventilator, syringe pumps, monitors, defibrillator, crash carts etc.

  • PURPOSE & SCOPE
    • Purpose:

To provide guideline instructions for in patient intensive / critical process with the aim that

      • Needs and expectations of patients are established
      • Patient satisfaction is enhanced on continual basis.
    • Scope:
      • It provides intensive care (treatment and monitoring) for people who are in a critically ill or unstable condition.
      • People in ICUs need constant medical support to keep their body functioning.
      • They may not be able to breathe on their own and they may have multiple organ failure.
      • Medical equipment takes the place of these functions while the person recovers.

  • DEFINITIONS
    • Advance life support:

Emergency medical care for sustaining life, including defibrillation, airway management, and drugs and medications

    • Adverse drug event:
      • Adverse event:

Any untoward medical occurrence that may present during treatment with a pharmaceutical product but which does not necessarily have a causal relationship with this treatment

      • Adverse Drug Reaction:

A response to a drug which is noxious and unintended and which occurs at doses normally used in man for prophylaxis, diagnosis, or therapy of disease or for the modification of physiologic function

Therefore ADR = Adverse Event with a causal link to a drug.

      • Adverse drug event:

The FDA recognizes the term adverse drug event to be a synonym for adverse event. In the patient-safety literature, the terms adverse drug event and adverse event usually denote a causal association between the drug and the event, but there is a wide spectrum of definitions for these terms, including harm caused by a

  • Drug
  • harm caused by drug use, and
  • a medication error with or without harm
    • Adverse events:

An injury related to medical management, in contrast to complications of disease. Medical management includes all aspects of care, including diagnosis and treatment, failure to diagnose or treat and the systems and equipment used to deliver care. Adverse events may be preventable or non-preventable.

(WHO Draft Guidelines for Adverse Event Reporting and Learning Systems)

    • Assessment:

All activities including history taking, physical examination, laboratory investigations that contribute towards determining the prevailing clinical status of the patient

    • Barrier nursing:

The nursing of patients with infectious diseases in isolation to prevent the spread of infection.

As the name implies, the aim is to erect a barrier to the passage of infectious pathogenic organisms between the contagious patient and other patients and staff in the hospital, and thence to the outside world.

The nurses wear gowns, masks, and gloves, and they observe strict rules that minimize the risk of passing on infectious agents.

    • Basic life support:

Basic life support (BLS) is the level of medical care which is used for patients with life-threatening illnesses or injuries until the patient can be given full medical care.

    • Confidentiality:

Restricted access to information to individuals who have a need, a reason and permission for such access

It also includes an individual‘s right to personal privacy as well as privacy of information related to his/her healthcare records.

    • Consent
      • Willingness of a party to undergo examination/procedure/ treatment by a healthcare provider. It may be implied (e.g. patient registering in OPD), expressed which may be written or verbal. Informed consent is a type of consent in which the healthcare provider has a duty to inform his/her patient about the procedure, its potential risk and benefits, alternative procedure with their risk and benefits so as to enable the patient to take an informed decision of his/her health care.
      • In law, it means active acquiescence or silent compliance by a person legally capable of consenting. In India, legal age of consent is 18 years. It may be evidenced by words or acts or by silence when silence implies concurrence. Actual or implied consent is necessarily an element in every contract and every agreement.
    • Drug Administration:

The giving of a therapeutic agent to a patient, e.g. by infusion, inhalation, injection, paste, suppository or tablet. It includes aerosol, oral, trans tracheal infusion, subcutaneous, intramuscular, intravenous, intrauterine, intraperitoneal, intraarticular, intramammary, intrathecal, subconjunctival, percutaneous, percutaneous intraruminal, gas inhalation. Mass medication is per feed or drinking water or, in the case of captive fish, in the tank water. For feral animals individual dosing by projectile dart is usual, for group therapy administration by bait is possible.

    • End of life Care:

Helps all those with advanced, progressive, incurable illness to live as well as possible until they die. It enables the supportive and palliative care needs of both patient and family to be identified and met throughout the last phase of life and into bereavement. It includes management of pain and other symptoms and provision of psychological, social, spiritual and practical support.

    • Family:

The person(s) with a significant role in the patient‘s life. It mainly includes spouse, children and parents. It may also include a person not legally related to the patient but can make healthcare decisions for a patient if the patient loses decision-making ability.

    • Healthcare associated Infections (HAI):

Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) are infections caused by a wide variety of common and unusual bacteria, fungi, and viruses during the course of receiving medical care. (CDC)

This was earlier referred to as Nosocomial / hospital-acquired / hospital-associated infection(s).

    • High Risk / High Alert Medications:

High-risk / high-alert medications can be defined as those drugs that have a heightened risk for adverse events or have heightened risk of catastrophic harm whenever there is an error. These drugs include generally have low therapeutic index.

    • Medication error:

A medication error is any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm while the medication is in the control of the health care professional, patient or consumer. Such events may be related to professional practice, health care products, procedures, and systems, including prescribing; order communication; product labeling, packing and nomenclature; compounding; dispensing; distribution; administration; education; monitoring; and use.

    • Re-assessment:

It implies continuous and on-going assessment of the patient which is recorded in the medical records as progress notes.

    • Special Educational needs of the patient:

In addition to routine carried by the healthcare professionals, patients and family have special educational needs depending on the situation. E.g.: a post-surgical patient who has to take care of his wound, NG tube feeding, Patient on tracheostomy getting discharged who has to be taken care by the family etc. The special educational needs are also greatly influenced by the literacy, educational level, language, emotional barriers and physical and cognitive limitations.

Hence it is important for the staff to determine the special educational needs and the challenges influencing the effective education.

    • Unstable patient:

A patient whose vital parameters need external assistance for their maintenance.

    • Ventilator Associated Adverse Events:
      • The new term, ventilator-associated event (VAE), groups all the conditions that result in a significant and sustained deterioration in oxygenation, (defined as a greater than 20% increase in the daily minimum fraction of inspired oxygen or an increase of at least 3 cm H2O in the daily minimum positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to maintain oxygenation).
      • It is imperative to understand that both infectious conditions (such as tracheitis, tracheobronchitis, and pneumonia) and non-infectious conditions (such as atelectasis, pulmonary embolism, pulmonary edema, ventilator-induced lung injury, and others) may fulfill this VAE definition.
      • The definition is 3 tiered, as follows:
        • Tier 1: ventilator-associated condition (VAC):

The patient develops hypoxemia (as defined above) for a sustained period of more than 2 days. The etiology of the hypoxemia is not considered.

        • Tier 2: infection-related ventilator-associated complication(IVAC):

Hypoxemia develops in the setting of generalized infection or inflammation, and antibiotics are instituted for a minimum of 4 days.

        • Tier 3: probable or possible ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP):

Additional laboratory evidence of white blood cells on Gram stain of material from a respiratory secretion specimen of acceptable quality, or (=possible) /and (=probable) presence of respiratory pathogens on quantitative cultures, in patients with IVAC. Additional criteria are also available for use in meeting the possible or Probable VAP (PVAP) definitions.

    • Vulnerable patient:

Those patients who are prone to injury and disease by virtue of their age, sex, physical, mental and immunological status, e.g. infants, elderly, physically- and mentally-challenged, semiconscious / unconscious, those on immunosuppressive and / or chemotherapeutic agents

    • Roles and responsibilities:
      • Position: Intensivist
        • Evaluate and treat new adult admissions and intervene to prevent further deterioration.
        • Diagnose and stabilize critically ill medical and surgical patients with impending or active organ failure (respiratory, cardiac, neurologic, hepatic, gastrointestinal, hematologic, renal, etc.) or life-threatening electrolyte and acid-base disturbances, or poisonings
        • Perform diagnostic-therapeutic procedures such as, central lines and dialysis catheters as consulted, that you have clinical privileges to perform. Document the procedure in the patient chart. All notes must be dated and timed.
        • Participate in the Medical Emergency Team (MET) or Rapid Response Team (RRT) per hospital policy.
        • Initiate advanced cardiac life support until the code team arrives, then supervise and support the code team.
        • Use data from appropriate monitoring devices to titrate therapy in the ICU.
        • Initiate, manage, and wean patients from mechanical ventilation using a variety of techniques and ventilators.
        • Act as the ICU team leader where appropriate and increase the clinical skill of ICU nurse practitioners, nurses and ancillary personnel in caring for critically ill patients.
        • Institute best practices
        • Sign-in and complete the time sheets daily
        • Respond to patient alarms and alerts
        • Proactively communicate changes in patient status to the appropriate physician(s)
        • Provide acute resuscitation for trauma and other emergencies when requested.
        • Effectively communicate with members of the virtual ICU team in a collegial manner to provide safe and error-free care during routine care and emergent conditions.
      • Position: Consultant
        • To provide state-of-the-art treatment of the critically ill patient in a 24 h coverage system for 7 continuous days at a time.
        • To ensure reasonable availability and rotation in the continuous on-call system.
        • To conduct at least two clinical rounds a day.
        • Being immediately available for urgent consultation and assistance in the resuscitation and subsequent management of critically ill patients.
        • Supervising trainees in the intensive care unit,
        • Provide acute resuscitation for trauma and other emergencies when requested.
        • Provide transport of critically ill patients when requested.
        • To be aware of unit admission and discharge criteria.
        • Administrative and research
        • Ensuring and reviewing quality of patient care by participating in audit, peer review and quality assurance programs.
        • Maintaining personal knowledge and skills by participating in continuing education and maintenance of professional standards programs.
        • Contributing to hospital committees, and the committees of health authorities and other organisations.
        • Ensuring research is carried out in the unit by participating in and/or supporting research.
      • Position: Resident Medical Officer (MBBS)
        • To provide medical treatment of the critically ill patient in a “shift duty” coverage system.
        • To ensure reasonable availability for the “shift duty” on-call system.
        • To be present at all relevant clinical rounds.
        • To follow departmental guidelines relating to routine clinical duties in the ICU.
        • To perform routine and emergency clinical procedures as indicated.
        • To be available to supervisors and medical colleagues for liaison regarding patient care.
        • To provide acute resuscitation for trauma and other emergencies when requested.
        • To provide transport of critically ill patients when requested.
        • To be aware of unit admission and discharge criteria.
        • To be aware of unit administration policy.
      • Position: Physician Assistant – Intensive Care Unit
        • Job Specification:
  • Qualification: Graduation: BAMS / BHMS

Post-Graduation: PGDEMS / DEMS (Additional)

Certifications: BLS & / or ACLS

  • Attention to Detail
        • ICU Patient Care Responsibilities:
  • To promptly attend to patients admitted in ICU.
  • To evaluate the medical needs of patients and facilitate all necessary measures for patient to receive appropriate care.
  • To place call to concerned Resident or Consultant on call based on the presenting complaint / condition of the patient.
  • To call for and check previous records if available.
  • To attend patients complaints and to calm patient/ relatives if apprehensive.
  • To assist in quick initiation of treatment of patients as per the consultants instructions.
  • To ensure the necessary consents before procedures.
  • To assist the Residents / Consultants in folleys catherization, ryles tube insertion, Pericardial tapping, ascitic or pleural tapping, IV cannulation, Endotrachial intubation, central line, Defibrillation
  • To observe and notify the Hemodynamic monitoring like HR, BP, SPO2, patients airway breathing circulation, intake output, ventilator parameters etc.
  • To assist in emergency management events for CPR, Defibrillation, Synchronized cardio-version etc.
  • To indent medicines online as per the Patient’s Prescription.
  • To give pathological, radiological investigations, blood components requisition forms to relatives
  • To complete the Clinical Documentation (accurate & complete) – initial assessment, Registers, Investigation Requisitions, transfer to ward format, other formats applicable to Department.
  • To inform the Patient / relatives regarding Condition of Patient, Likely Hospital Stay and do Financial Counseling.
  • To write down the treatment sheet for the next day in the night duty.
  • To prepare Discharge Summary / DAMA of the patient for the consultant who do not have physician assistant / residents.
  • To record the patients vital parameters in each shift as per protocol.
  • To ensure proper handing over from one shift to other.
  • To announce hospital wide codes as necessary.
  • In case of expired patient, to fill the Death Certificate, MLC intimation, Death Summary, Corporation Form, after patient's death and hand over it to the patient's relative after proper billing and as per hospital protocol.
        • General Responsibilities:
  • To follow the duty schedule and to take prior permission of functional head in case of any mutual arrangements/ leaves etc.
  • To carry out responsibility as advised by the superiors from time to time
  • To maintain necessary records of the Department
  • To work in harmonious environment and promote team work with your colleagues all the time
  • To be responsible for department activities and to take initiatives for continuous improvement.
  • To update self-knowledge and competence for the current protocols
  • To follow appropriate formal dress code and code of conduct.
  • To be regularly trained on all mandatory Trainings topics as organized by the HR Department from time to time.
  • To be trained in BLS and ACLS as per recommended intervals.
  • To ensure complete understanding of the departmental manual & SOP’s and to participate in the regular updating of the same.

  • QUALITY GOAL AND OBJECTIVE
    • Goals of the ICU department:
      • Establishing and incorporating of rules, procedures, work flow and protocols for the smooth and efficient functioning of the department and performance.
      • Provision of an ideal environment for conducting procedure by:
        • Promoting a high standard of asepsis
        • Ensuring proper care and comfort of patients
        • Providing optimum conditions of work for staff.
      • Prevention of Procedural complications by:
        • Ensuring a high standard of safety and safeguarding of patients and staff respectively
        • Ensuring immediate care of patients
      • Promoting rational use of devices by Intensivist, Consultant and nurses.
    • Objectives of the ICU department
      • To ensure close communication and co-ordination between ICU and Other department
      • To foster a high degree of work discipline among staff members
      • To streamline the general routines to be adhered to
      • To ensure care and availability of equipments and facilities
      • To promote optimum utilization of Beds, Equipment and staff
      • To ensure there is proper communication and maintenance of information
      • To develop effective policies for patient safety
      • To provide skilled, efficient & appropriate care to the patients admitted with a humane touch and personalized attention
      • Training & documentation of all Doctors, Intensivists & ICU sisters.
      • Safe & effective sterilization & fumigation procedure.
      • Improving coordination among the doctors, nurses and the Intensivists.
      • Having control of the stock available in the ICUs; assigning work to different people & verifying them at regular intervals.
      • Streamlining of various processes related to Consumable Procurement & Billing.
      • To reduce the rate of infection to the minimum possible standards.
      • Evidence of catheter related sepsis, catheter related infection, inadvertent tracheal extubation, accidental central line removal, reintubation rate & readmission rate. Should be zero or less than 1%.

Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Admission Process
Policy Code:___________ICU_04NABH Standard No.:COP.09.b
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU
Aim
To define and streamline the process of booking and allotment of beds
Responsibility
RMO / Physician’s Assistant
Nursing Staff
Procedure
If the patient is being shifted from casualty
The CMO will inform the details of patient condition and the treatment advised by consultant to ICU RMO / Physician’s Assistant
If the patient is severely ill, then CMO will accompany the patient till ICU
Casualty staff nurse will inform the condition and treatment to be followed by ICU staff nurse.
Casualty nurse will accompany the patient while shifting with file of the patient.
The patient will be shifted to ICU within 10 minutes after stabilizing.
If the patient is being shifted from the ward
Ward RMO will inform the details of patient condition and the treatment advised by consultant to ICU RMO.
The ward staff nurse will inform the condition and treatment to be followed to ICU staff nurse.
The ward nurse will accompany the patient while shifting with file of the patient.
On arrival of a patient to ICU
ICU RMO will quickly assess the patient and inform to Intensivist and the consultant of the patient.
Hospital cloths will be given to the patient and leads and blood pressure cuff will be attached to patient and the monitor vitals. ICU RMO / staff nurse will confirm pulse / temperature / blood pressure manually.
ICU RMO will obtain history from the patient / relatives (if needed) and will write down the case history / medicine order in history sheet as advised by the consultant / Intensivist.
ICU staff nurse will follow the instructions given by ICU RMO / Intensivist.
ICU RMO will assess the condition of the patient time to time/ whenever required and will inform to the consultant / Intensivist.
ICU staff nurse will inform any change in the condition of a patient to ICU RMO.
Informing relatives about the condition of the patient
After assessing the patient, ICU RMO / Intensivist will brief about the condition of a patient to the relatives.
The consultant in charge will also discuss the condition and further management with patient and the relatives.
Before any clinical procedure, ICU RMO / Intensivist / Consultant will inform the patient and relatives about the procedure and consent will be obtained by ICU staff nurse.
Documentation:
All admissions to the ICU should be documented in the ICU register.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Discharge Process
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_05NABH Standard No.:COP.09.b
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU
Aim
To define and streamline the process of discharge
Responsibility
RMO / Physician’s Assistant
Nursing Staff
Procedure
Procedure - normal discharge:
Discharge is advised by the consultant / intensivist and documented
Patient and companion are explained about discharge procedure by nurse.
Drugs and medical supplies shall be refunded
Dietary department to be informed and counselling if required shall be done by the dietician.
Nurse checks for all tests and procedure entries in the system and collects reports
IP case sheet is sent to the Billing department after clearance from the pharmacy and medical supplies.
Nurse checks with the relatives for the mode of transportation. If needed, helps them to arrange for transportation.
RMO / Residents prepares the discharge summary
Nurse keeps the patient’s record ready with all the reports.
When the bill is generated from the Billing department, the nurse directs the patient’s companion to the billing counter for clearance.
For Insurance patients an extra copy of the discharge summary is generated
The nurse’s explains the discharge summary, after care treatment and follow up instructions to the patient and the attender.
It is ensured that the ID band and IV cannula are removed
Nurse hands over the discharge file with discharge summary and other reports to patient / attender & signature of acknowledgement of the same is obtained in the admission & discharge register
It is ensured that no patient is discharged unless accompanied by a companion.
Nurse checks that all the records are complete for dispatch to MRD.
It is ensured that terminal disinfection of the unit is done and the unit kept ready to receive the next patient.
Procedure - DAMA (discharge against medical advice):
Consultant / intensivist is informed regarding patient’s desire to leave the hospital against medical advice.
The consultant / intensivist explain the risk and consequences of leaving the hospital to the patient and companion
Consultant / intensivist document in the progress notes of the patient that the patient and companion have been informed about the risks and consequences of leaving the hospital against medical advice.
Obtain the consent from patient / companion on the DAMA form.
Proceed with the formalities of discharge procedure.
Assist the patient / attender for transportation to other hospital / place of their destination.
Ensure that no I V line / catheter is present on the patient. If patient is required for continuity of care, confirm with the consultant & document the same in progress notes.
Documentation:
All transfers / discharges from the ICU should be documented in the ICU register.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Transfer of patients
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_06NABH Standard No.:COP.09.b
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU
Purpose
To establish an appropriate mechanism & provide with guidelines for safe transfer of patients from ICU.
To maintain the continuity of care after transfer from ICU to ward.
Responsibility
ICU physician
In-nursing in-charge
ICU Assigned Nurse
Receiving Nurse
Equipment
IV stand
Cardiac Monitor
Defibrillator
Pulse oxymeter
Oxygen cylinder
Policy
Status of the patient shall be assessed by ICU physician in-charge for stabilization of patient’s physiologic status and when the need for ICU monitoring and care is no longer necessary.
The ICU physician in-charge makes decision to transfer / discharge the patient from ICU.
Discharge of the patient may include assessment of functional, medical, medication, psychological, and / or cultural needs.
Transfer / discharge planning from ICU are a multidisciplinary, collaborative process involving the patient, patient’s family and concerned team members.
There should be written ICU physician order before patient’s transfer out.
Inform the patient and family about the transfer unless in emergency situation.
The patient should be transferred out to another area accompanied by an ICU nurse.
Procedure
ICU physician in-charge shall order for the discharge / transfer out of the patient to ward from ICU, He shall design detailed plan of management, treatment and care to be followed in ward.
ICU Nursing in-charge will reserve bed in the specified ward and inform receiving ward nursing in-charge about patient condition, patient’s specific medical requirements, and necessary preparation for receiving the patient.
The ICU RMO will write ICU transfer note and revised physician orders in patient medical record. The discharge summary will contain, but not limited to:
Reason for admission.
Significant findings.
Diagnosis.
Condition at discharge.
Investigation results.
Details of any procedure performed.
Medication given.
Other treatment given.
Follow up medication.
Any special care needed e.g. to watch for drainage tubes, strict intake output charting or frequent blood sugar monitoring with specified frequency of time etc.
The Nursing in-charge, Assigned Nurse and as well as the ICU physician are responsible for coordinating the discharge with other team members.
ICU physician will inform his team members about the transfer and special care or needs (if any).
The ICU physician ensures that the receiving team on the floor is well informed about the patient’s status and on-going patient needs.
After all the communication and documentations, the assigned nurse will do the following:
Explain the patient about ward situation if patient is conscious.
Arrange patient’s file according to the hospital policy (The file will be arranged by the ward clerk, if available).
Fill up transfer check list and confirm all documents in the file.
Give due medicines till the patient leaves the unit.
Check the vital signs before transfer the patient, if any changes inform ICU physician.
Equip patient’s bed with the entire patient’s requirements i.e. portable hemodynamic monitor, pulse oxymeter, oxygen cylinder etc.
Assigned nurse ensures that all the cardiac electrodes are well placed.
To empty all the fluid collection bags, if present e.g. urobag, chest tube drainage, abdominal drainage or any other drains, to avoid leakage, as well as correct measurement in the ward.
If patient is on tracheostomy tube, then do suction immediately before transfer.
Preferably shift the patient on his / her own bed i.e. not on stretcher.
Endorse / handover the patient to the receiving ward nurse, and give complete and accurate information with patient’s full documents:
Patient data
History of illness- if referral from other hospital, state the name of the hospital
Medications, treatments, IV Fluids
Vital signs
Any invasive lines
Any special procedures like CT, ultrasound, and others
Whether intubation and mechanical ventilation was done
With or without oxygen
Diet
Post-operative patients-operation site, wound dressing
Activity in the ward
Skin condition of the patient
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Admission & Discharge Criteria in ICU
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_07NABH Standard No.:COP.09.b
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU
Purpose:
To provide guideline for admission & discharge criteria in ICU
Responsibility:
Treating consultants
Intensivist
Admission Criteria:
Admission criteria based on medical conditions:
Unstable patients requiring intensive treatment & monitoring that cannot be provided outside of the ICU
Patients requiring ventilator support, continuous vasoactive drug infusions etc.
Post-operative, after major surgeries.
Acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilator support.
Patients in shock.
Patients with chronic co morbid conditions who develop acute severe medical or surgical illness.
Patients with metastatic malignancy complicated by infection, cardiac tamponade or airway obstruction.
Hemo-dynamically unstable patients receiving invasive monitoring; Such as:
Pulse less than 40 or more than 150 beats / minute
Systolic arterial pressure less than 80 mm Hg or 20 mm Hg below the patient’s usual pressure.
Mean arterial pressure less than 60 mm Hg
Diastolic arterial pressure more than 120 mm Hg
Respiratory rate more than 35 breaths / minute
Admission criteria based on specific conditions / diseases:
Medical ICU:
Pulmonary System
Acute respiratory failure (PaO2 less than 50 mm Hg) or (PCO2 > 45mmHg with respiratory acidosis) requiring ventilator support.
Patients in wards who are demonstrating respiratory deterioration.
Need for nursing / respiratory care not available in lesser care areas such as wards
Massive hemoptysis
Drug Ingestion and Drug Overdose

Prioritization model:
This system defines those that will benefit most from the ICU (Priority 1) to those that will not benefit at all (Priority4) from ICU admission.
Priority 1:
These are critically ill, unstable patients in need of intensive treatment and monitoring that cannot be provided outside of the ICU.
Usually, these treatments include ventilator support, continuous vasoactive drug infusions, etc.
Priority 1 patients generally have no limits placed on the extent of therapy they are to receive.
Examples of these patients may include post-operative/ trauma or acute respiratory failure patients requiring mechanical ventilator support and hemo-dynamically unstable patients receiving invasive monitoring and/or vasoactive drugs.
Priority 2:
These patients require intensive monitoring and may potentially need immediate intervention.
No therapeutic limits are generally stipulated for these patients.
Examples include patients with chronic comorbid conditions who develop acute severe medical or surgical illness.
Priority 3:
These unstable patients are critically ill but have a reduced likelihood of recovery because of underlying disease or nature of their acute illness.
Priority 3 patients may receive intensive treatment to relieve acute illness but limits on therapeutic efforts may be set such as no intubation or cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
Examples include patients with metastatic malignancy complicated by infection, cardiac tamponade, or airway obstruction.
Priority 4:
These are patients who are generally not appropriate for ICU admission. Admission of these patients should be on an individual basis, under unusual circumstances and at the discretion of the Medical Director. These patients can be placed in the following categories:
Little or no anticipated benefit from ICU care based on low risk of active intervention that could not safely be administered in a non-ICU setting (too well to benefit from ICU care).
Examples include patients with peripheral vascular surgery, hemo-dynamically stable diabetic ketoacidosis, mild congestive heart failure, conscious drug overdose etc.
Patients with terminal and irreversible illness facing imminent death (too sick to benefit from ICU care).
For example: severe irreversible brain damage, irreversible multi-organ system failure, metastatic cancer unresponsive to chemotherapy and/or radiation therapy (unless the patient is on a specific treatment protocol), patients with decision-making capacity who decline intensive care and/or invasive monitoring and who receive comfort care only, brain dead non-organ donors, patients in a persistent vegetative state, patients who are permanently unconscious, etc.
Discharge / Transfer:
Patient in the ICU should be discharged / transferred out after detailed review and evaluation of the clinical condition by the treating physician as well as the HOD of ICU.
It should be ensured that the disease process or the critical unstable physiological condition, for which the patient was admitted, has been reversed and the patient no longer requires intensive monitoring therapy.
Some of the criteria for discharge transfer from ICU are as follows:
Hemodynamic parameters stable and within the acceptable range.
All monitoring catheters are removed.
Cardiac activity- rate and rhythm stable and within acceptable range. Patient not on inotropic/ anti arrhythmic or any other intravenous drugs.
Patent airway, arterial blood gas stable and within normal range. Normal spontaneous respiration with minimal oxygen inhalation. No respiratory distress.
Metabolic imbalance corrected and patient stable.
Patient should be neurologically stable.
ICU patients, being still sick are generally not discharged to home but transferred to other acute ward. The important thing to decide is whether the patient is well enough and safely manageable with the level of care available in the acute ward. If yes, the patient may be transferred out of ICU.
There may be situations where the ICU care cannot be of any further benefit to the patient either because the pathology has become irreversible or because the recovery would be a long process. In such situations the relatives may be briefed and the patient discharged from ICU to avoid any unnecessary expenditure or bed occupancy.
A patient being transferred out to another ICU, should be fully evaluated (all parameters recorded,) patient’s condition and the risks en route fully explained to the next of kin and recorded in the discharge notes. Consent should be obtained from the next of kin that the risks to life of patient have been fully explained and he/she is getting discharged against medical advice.

Discharge / Transfer Criteria:
Purpose
To streamline the entire discharge process with maximum efficiency
Discharge Criteria
The status of the patient admitted to the ICU should be constantly monitored to identify those who may no longer need ICU care.
Discharge from ICU is considered when the patient’s vitals and physiological status are stabilized and close monitoring and care are no longer necessary.
When a patient’s illness is so terminal and physiological status has deteriorated and active intervention is no more planned, discharge can be initiated on the patient’s companion’s request.
Discharge criteria to guide discharge patients from ICU:
Stable uncomplicated hemo-dynamically stable myocardial infarction after 48 hrs.
Any hemo-dynamically stable dysrhythmias.
Congestive cardiac failure patients stable and not in shock (killip class I, II).
Hypertensive emergencies with stabilized blood pressure.
Respiratory System:
Medically stable patient off ventilator for at least 24 hours and the primary etiology for which patient was ventilated has resolved.
Patient’s whose hypoxia is under control and needs only occasional physiotherapy.
Absence of copious secretion requiring suction frequency more than once in two hours.
Drug over dose and poisoning
Patients who are stable and need only infrequent observation.
Endocrine System and Metabolism related
Recovered diabetic ketoacidosis stable but requiring only blood sugar monitoring.
Hyperosmolar state with resolution of coma.
Thyrotoxicosis and hypothyroid cases stabilized.
Miscellaneous Conditions
Septic shock whose primary infection is controlled and is hemo-dynamically stable.
Gastrointestinal disorders
G I bleeds which are under control.
Recovered liver failure with stable signs.
Neurological Disorders
Patients with established and stable stroke or traumatic brain injury who require only occasional neurological assessment or only minimal suctioning and turning in bed with a GCS above 9.
Stable neuro muscular disorders not requiring ventilator support.
Surgical
Post-operative cases those are stable after 24 hours.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Post-surgical Bed
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_08NABH Standard No.:COP.09.a
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU
Policy
Post-surgical procedure patients have the utmost priority for ICU bed utilization.
Proper procedures should be followed to reserve a bed for a post-surgical patient for better utilization of ICU beds
All surgical procedure patients must have a booked reserved bed on the hospital ward in order to reserve a bed in ICU.
Emergency surgical procedures are an exception to the above rule.
All planned elective surgeries must have a reserved bed before starting the surgical procedure.
Procedure
The surgical team must book in the booking book, a bed, a minimum of one night before the surgical procedure by either calling the nursing in-charge or the nurses’ station or the ICU team leader.
On the day of the surgical procedure, the team or anaesthetist must call the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) or the team leader to reconfirm the bed request and get the bed location.
In case of changes to the patient status when the ICU bed is no longer needed, it is the responsibility of the team or anaesthetist to cancel the request.
In the case of an emergency, the surgical team or anaesthetist should call the consultant in charge in the ICU (look him up at the rota) for immediate confirmation or page the team leader on-call in the ICU. The ICU team leader should take the approval of the intensivist and get back to the requesting team.
In case of the following, a bed in ICU for elective procedures may not be guaranteed:
If the booking was not made the night before to ensure adequate time to provide nursing coverage
If the above procedure was not followed.
In case the bed was booked and no ICU bed was available on the day of surgery, an incident report should be filled and sent to Quality department.
The above rule does not apply for infected patients.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for handling of bed shortage
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_09NABH Standard No.:COP.09.e
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU

Aim:
To provide guidelines for handling of bed shortage in ICU
Procedure:
As and when there are shortages of beds in the ICU and there is a requirement of such beds, then the following procedure shall be implemented as per the situation:
If there is no vacant bed in the ICU but bed is available in any other high dependency units, then the patient requiring such bed shall be shifted there.
If there is only one bed available and number of patients requiring beds is more than one, then the admission criteria will be as per the prioritization and collaborative decision taken by the intensivist and the treating consultants.
If there is no vacant bed in any of the ICUs then the patient / relatives shall be informed about the situation and they shall be helped to transfer the patient to ICU units of any nearby healthcare facility.
The patient shall be shifted to emergency department and till the necessary arrangements are made and transfer takes place.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Infection Control
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_10NABH Standard No.:COP.09.f, HIC.02.a
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU
Purpose
To prevent the cross-transmission of infection between patients, Health Care Workers (HCW) and visitors in ICU.
To reduce morbidity and mortality of patients and personnel by preventing and/or reducing exposure to infectious agents.
Responsibility
Infection control Team
All Staff in ICU
Equipment
Mask
Gown
Cap
Soap
Alcohol Hand Scrub
Policy
Adequate precautions should be taken by all ICU staff, based on each patient’s diagnosis / condition, to protect both patients and their visitors from exposure to any infectious contaminates.
Personnel who are at risk, due to immune suppression or other communicable infections, should not have direct contact with ICU patients.
Visitors with a noticeable illness (common colds, flu, etc.) should be restricted from the patient care areas.
Food or drink other than patient food should not be allowed inside the ICU.
Staff should notify his/her supervisor when exposure to blood / body fluid occurs.
Staff compliance to Infection Control practices should be monitored by Infection Control practitioner.
Any significant findings or trends are reported to the Infection Control Head, ICU Head Nurse
Procedure
Following measures for prevention and control of infections in ICU shall be taken
Health Standards for Personnel:
Personnel who are at risk, due to immune suppression or other communicable infections, should not have direct contact with ICU patients.
Nursing staff who, because of current health conditions are unable to utilize the standard precautions e.g., rash on hands and cannot use gloves, will be evaluated
The ICU Head Nurse will be responsible for advising personnel of exposure to airborne pathogens, as well as obtaining information requested from Infection Control representatives.
Each employee is responsible for notify his/her supervisor when exposure to blood/body fluid occurs.
ICU personnel who have concerns or questions regarding the risk of acquiring infections.
Standard Precautions:
Hand hygiene: Wash hands before initiating contact with patients, and when body substances have soiled the hands. Hands are to be washed with soap or hospital approved antiseptic agent, running water and friction for 10 seconds, paying particular attention to around and under fingernails and between the fingers. Hands should be washed thoroughly and immediately if they accidentally become contaminated.
Gloves should be changed between each patient and/or each task involving blood and/or body substances.
Protective barrier gown shall be worn whenever contamination of clothing or arms with blood or body substances is anticipated.
Face masks shield and/or eye protection devices are to be worn during tasks where splashing, splattering or spraying with body substance is anticipated, i.e., line placement, suctioning, etc.
Sharps such as scalpels and needles will be disposed of in the approved sharps container.
Management of Patient with Resistant Organisms:
In the Intensive Care Units, when multiple drug resistant bacteria are cultured from any site, the need for isolation/transfer will be evaluated in consultation with the Infection Control Specialist and/or the physician. The following organisms are examples:
Gram negative bacilli resistant to Gentamycin, Amikacin or Tobramycin.
Methicillin (Oxacillin) Resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA
Steptococcus pneumonia resistant to penicillin.
Pan-resistant organisms.
Precautions:
Standard Precaution (including the use of gloves) should be used for all patient contact.
Contact Precaution should be used in care of patient with resistant organisms.
Precautions will be maintained until:
Two negative cultures are obtained from the original site at least 72 hours apart and following completion of effective therapy (negative culture is defined as a report of “no growth”, “normal flora” an organism which does not confirm to any of the preceding definitions).
If unable to obtain culture: continue precautions at least one week after discontinuation of all antibiotics.
If not treated: Two negative cultures are obtained from the original site at least 72 hours apart, at least one week following collection date of original isolate.
If unable to obtain culture and not treated:
One week after resolution of clinical signs of infection.
Nursing personnel should document in the patient’s plan of care that standard precautions & contact precautions are in use for patients with resistant organisms.
When a resistant organism is isolated from any site, in two or more patients on the same unit, the Infection Control department will be consulted and an epidemiological investigation will be initiated, if indicated.
Management of Outbreak:
Cluster epidemiology will become the immediate top priority at any time an unexpected occurrence or frequency of infection becomes evident.
The nurse is to report infection clusters or unusual patterns (especially viral or parasitic infection).
Indicators for such increased incidence may include reports of a particular organism, service, site or unit.
All infections which fit the previously mentioned criteria will be reported to the Infection Control Specialist.
The outbreak investigation is to be directed by Infection Control staff with cooperation of nursing staff
The type of control measures and their duration (e.g., closure of unit or closure to new admissions) will be determined by the Chairperson of the Infection Control Committee.
If diversion of new admits is required, they will be located in an Intensive Care environment which can best meet their treatment needs.
The decision to close a unit or limit admission in the event of an outbreak will be made
Assignment of nursing personnel:
Nursing personnel shall be given patient care assignments which minimize the risk of transmission of infectious organisms, if at all possible.
In the event such assignments are not possible, patients will be grouped, based on infectious agents / colonizing organisms to minimize the spread of accidental transmission.
Isolation precautions for patients:
If nursing personnel suspects a patient requires isolation precautions:
Contact the ICU physician.
Obtain confirmation of diagnosis.
Initiate isolation precautions, as indicated.
Document in patient’s medical record.
Evaluate and document patient’s response to intervention.
Call Infection Control Specialist to assist with special needs required.
Physicians should document patient’s diagnosis of a defined airborne disease in patient’s medical record.
Isolation / Private Rooms:
An isolation / private room can reduce the possibility of transmission of infectious agents.
The type of infection, patient’s clinical manifestation; infectious source and mode of transmission are factors to be considered when determining the need for a private room.
Cardiac / Medical / Surgical intensive care patients requiring airborne precautions should be placed in a private room with a door.
Isolation / Private rooms should be provided when soiling with body substances is excessive.
Room determination shall be made without regard to diagnosis
If the unit cannot follow special precautions for any reason the Infection Control Specialist will be notified.
Transport of Patients with Infectious Disease:
Communicate with the receiving department about the patient current infectious status when a patient with an infectious disease requires transport out of the ICU.
During transport all non-essential personnel should not have contact with the patient.
When preparing the patient for transport, the staff should create a closed system as much as possible.
Consideration should be given for discontinuation of any equipment not necessary for the patient’s short term care needs.
Invasive lines should be secured to minimize the potential for body substance contamination.
Intubated patients requiring oxygen should be transported in a way which minimizes the potential for respiratory contamination.
Non-intubated patients requiring respiratory isolation will wear a mask all the time when off their unit or during transport.
Infection Control Guidelines for Visitors:
Nursing personnel are responsible for ensuring that adequate precautions are taken based on each patient’s diagnosis / condition, to protect both the patients and their visitors from exposure to any infectious contaminates.
Infection Control Practitioner / staff nurse will instruct visitor about standard precautions, hand washing, gowning, gloving, etc. as indicated.
Nursing personnel should restrict visitors with a noticeable illness (common colds, flu, etc.) in the patient care areas.
Staff should evaluate the appropriateness of the visit to prevent patients from exposure to communicable diseases.
Staff will inform a visitor when exposure would potentially affect the patient’s condition adversely and request they leave the area.
Traffic Control:
All visitors should enter/exit a unit from the main entrance following the hospital/unit visitor protocol.
In the unit, their contact shall be limited to whomever they have come to see.
No visitors will be allowed access to any other patient area or where medication, intravenous or wound care supplied is prepared or stored.
Environmental Hygiene:
The patient care areas should be cleaned daily, upon patient discharge & as needed utilizing hospital approved disinfectants; however frequency & cleaning schedule may change according to the housekeeping policy.
Any instrument which has been in contact with oral mucosa (laryngoscope blades and stylets) shall be confined and contained at the point of use in clear plastic bags labelled with bio hazardous insignia. This is exchanged with clean equipment.
Contaminated instruments and trays should be confined and contained at the point of use.
Equipment requiring sterilization and disinfection is the responsibility of Central Service Sterilization Department (CSSD).
Crash Cart – the inside of the crash cart should be cleaned periodically and supplies replaced when out-dated. The above items will be cleaned with a hospital approved solution.
All scissors, haemostats and similar instruments should be placed in clear plastic bags with a bio hazardous label & to be transported in a tray from “dirty” area.
Refrigerators- ICU staff will contact Housekeeping Department to schedule a time for refrigerator to be cleaned.
ICU staff will remove all items from the medication refrigerator and wipe up any spills.
Housekeeping staff will then clean all surfaces and defrost the freezer.
ICU staff is responsible for cleaning/rinsing items such as measuring cups and bedpans between their uses.
Food or drink other than patient food items will be kept outside the ICU.
General Equipment – items including tables, chairs, gurneys, scales, slider boards and monitor cables should be cleaned as soon as possible with approved solution and by appropriate staff.
Patient Discharge:
ICU staff will remove all items such as linen, patient care supplies, etc., which may have been contaminated by body substances.
Monitor cables and lead wires will be cleaned by ICU staff, with an approved solution.
Infusion pumps or equipment used at the bedside will be removed, obvious spills, wiped clean and the appropriate service area contacted for disinfection.
IV poles will be removed from the bedside and placed in the dirty utility room for cleaning.
Housekeeping staff will clean the area and prepare for the next admission.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for End of Life Situation
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_11NABH Standard No.:COP.22
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU

POLICY:
General Policies:
Terminally ill patients shall be provided appropriate pain and palliative care according to the wishes of family and patient.
Concerned staff shall address unique needs such as religious and socio-cultural beliefs of such patients and family.
If the body of the deceased is subjected to an autopsy or for organ donation, concerned doctor shall discuss this with family in courteous manner and after discussing with management necessary arrangements shall be done by the hospital for that purpose.
Policies To Guide The End Of Life Care:
The treating Consultant shall be the authorized person to start with the End of Life Care.
To communicate with the patient and / or family end of life care (EOLC) options and Empower them to fully participate in the decision making process.
This includes:
All types of end of life situations: sudden and unexpected, steady decline or slow decline marked by periodic crises;
Patient centered decision making or advance care planning may include provisions for: Living Will, Life Support, Refusal of Treatment, Organ Donation etc.
To provide opportunities for discussion and decision making between the patient, family and Health care team related to the emotional and physical effects of EOLC.
PROCEDURE:
Legal Requirements:
Decisions like ‘Do not resuscitate’ / ‘Do not intubate’ / ‘Allow natural death’ etc. shall be only as per the statutory laws and within the guidelines framed by the legal system.
Essential services available to those who need them include:
Providing appropriate pain and palliative care according to the wishes of the family and patient;
Sensitively addressing such issues as autopsy and organ donation;
Respecting the patient‘s values, religion and cultural preferences;
Involving the patient and family in all aspects of care; and
Responding to the psychological, emotional, spiritual and cultural concerns of the patient and family (where possible).
General Information:
Patients may designate a Surrogate Decision Maker to direct the course of their medical treatment in the event they have lost decision-making capacity.
Privacy should be provided by keeping the patient either in the private room or if it is in the ward separated by a screen.
Should clarify the questions asked by the patient truthfully.
Put the patient in a comfortable position and change the position frequently.
Identify the unique needs of the patient like religious prayer, support the family.
An imminent death may be denied by the family, the staff can help the family by such actions as ensuring them privacy, permitting them access to patients and showing them some kindness for their comfort as well as to the patient’s comfort.
Helping the patient to die in a dignified and peaceful manner is one of the most valuable contributions for the comfort of the patient and relatives.
Autopsy:
All MLC Registered patients death shall be subjected to Autopsy and therefore to be informed to the area civil police for necessary post mortem.
Any other death cases for which the Autopsy is requested by the relatives or the hospital authorities decide for the same, this procedure will be followed.
Organ Donation:
If the hospital authorities is informed about the organ donation done by the dying patient the arrangements shall be made to contact the organ collecting authorities to complete this process with the permission of the relatives.
Issues are addressed sensitively
Symptomatic Treatment:
Symptomatic treatment is provided and where appropriate measures are taken for the alleviation of pain.
The emphasis shall be on providing symptomatic treatment of such patients and to prevent complications to the possible extent.
The patient and / or family shall be involved while taking all such decisions. To the extent possible (and as per the law), the patient and / or family‘s choices shall be respected.
Pain Management:
The approach to pain management is the same regardless of what the terminal illness is.
Treatment must be individualized because patients perceive pain differently, depending in part on such factors as fatigue, insomnia, anxiety, depression, and nausea. A supportive environment can also help manage pain.
The most available and appropriate analgesic given by the least invasive route possible should be chosen.
Choice of an analgesic depends largely on pain intensity. Analgesics should be administered regularly rather than as needed; controlling pain after it recurs is more difficult than preventing it, partly because pain generates anxiety.
Anorexia:
Anorexia, common among dying patients, is usually more distressing to family members than to the patient. Counseling may be needed to help family / members accept anorexia and understand the futility of tube feedings or parenteral nutrition.
Some steps can be taken to increase a patient's food intake. For example, if a full meal tray is overwhelming, small portions, specially prepared foods, and a flexible meal schedule are recommended. A small amount of a favorite alcoholic beverage served 30 minutes before meals may help. Foods with strong flavors or smells sometimes stimulate the appetite.
Care Of The Body After Death:
As soon as the patient has breathed last, nurse should gently close his / her eyes and mouth if they are not already closed.
The body is placed flat on the bed with legs quite straight and arms laid at the sides.
A folded towel is used to prop up the chin in position for a short time or bandage can be used to hold the jaw firm.
Ankles are securely fastened together with a bandage to prevent their falling apart.
Ask the relatives to remove all jewelries (if any) and then list them, keep in separate package and pack along with other valuables.
Drainage tubes (if any) should be removed.
Then the patient should be cleaned completely and hair combed and dressed.
Then the rectum and vagina and all orifices are plugged with cotton to prevent the escape of the secretions when the muscles become relaxed.
Body is covered with a dead body cover.
An identification tag containing the patient age, address, UHID, ward no., bed no., and date and time of death is attached to one wrist.
Then the body is handed over to the relatives by taking signature with address of the receiving relatives with the permission of the doctor.
The room should be cleaned as early as possible.
The physician fills the death certificates before the body is handed over.
In-charge nurse should see that the death records are filled & completed before the body is handed over to the relatives.
Training of staff:
As regards the end of life care all concerned staff is to be educated to carry out the same. (Refer: Annexure)
ANNEXURE: Fact sheet on ‘End Of Life Care
What is End of Life Care?
End of life care is a person centered, personalized and family oriented perception of ‘Good Death’ which encompasses all aspects of comprehensive care of an individual at his or her end of life.
End of Life Care constitutes:
Applicability to any person, any place and any illness
Relief of physical, Psychological, Social, Spiritual and Existential symptoms
Dying at the preferred place of choice and receiving appropriate care by a trained health care Provider
Universal access to standard palliative care at end of life and every individual having a right to good, peaceful and dignified death of life care at ICU can be with de-escalation of life sustaining as in the ward setting, it can be with symptomatic care. The be transferred to hospice or home for provision of end of life
Modalities of End of life care at ICU can be with de-escalation of life sustaining measures, where as in the ward setting, it can be with symptomatic care. The patients can also be transferred to hospice or home for provision of end of life care.
What does documented procedure for End of Life Care mean?
End of life care document shall be a policy statement that facilitates a dignified dying process for those who are diagnosed to be at their end of life. It may consists of:
Documented Evidence:
Evidence of discussion, decision, communication, care provided etc. as documented in the medical case records
Goals of Care:
Discussion, decision and documentation of further goals of care with respect to site and nature of care
EOLC Management Plan:
It comprises of consensus EOLC decision by health care providers, EOLC communication, EOLC shared decision making, symptom control, managing the dying process, death and after death care including bereavement
When is End of Life Care applicable?
Whenever, the treating physicians or group of physicians feel that the medical care is FUTILE, then End of Life Care management can be discussed and initiated.
Medical futility is a clinical decision, which is defined as medical interventions that are unlikely to provide any significant clinical benefit for the patient.
The reference is to clinical situations where in absence of brain death, the physician believes that continuing life support is futile.
How patient management is continued at End of Life Care?
Patient management is done through symptom control which includes control of end of life symptoms such as pain, dyspnea, delirium, respiratory secretions, dryness of mouth etc.
Does all End of Life Care process happen in the ICU?
No.
Any area within the hospital premises that offers a private conducible and peaceful environment for the person to die and family members to be around can offer End of Life Care process.
It can be in ICU or in the ward. It will be preferable to provide the scope of religious clerics to attend and practice any rituals.
How Code of Medical Ethics facilitates End of Life Care decision making?
Patient Autonomy:
Means the Right to Self-determination, where the informed patient has a right to choose the manner of his treatment.
Beneficence:
It implies acting in what is (or judged to be) in patient's best interest.
Non-malfeasance:
Means to do no harm, to impose no unnecessary or unacceptable burden upon the patient
Distributive Justice:
Means that patients in similar circumstances should receive similar care
How Quality assurance be assessed during End of Life Care?
Quality Assurance in EOLC is governed by Quality of death. Quality of death is family / care givers appreciation of good death or family satisfaction of good end of life care processes.
It can be determined by following questions being asked to family members on quality of death (Rating 1-10):
Having pain and other symptoms under control
Having information about the illness, management and prognosis if this was desired
Having control over the treatment decisions and what was going on
Was able to meet and spend time with near and dear ones if desired
If a desire to die in hospital, home or hospice was met if it was requested
Non beneficial transfer to ICU or ICU or use or prolongation of life support measures in case of medical futility was avoided
Had access to religious, spiritual and any other wishes being fulfilled if it was desired
Died with loved ones present around
Died with dignity and respect
Can there be an independent system of monitoring End of Life Care process?
Healthcare organization can constitute Bio Ethics committee where in medical futility can be discussed by a group of expert stake holders (clinicians, nursing staff, medical social workers etc.) and the clinical consensus statement is agreed upon by family members (nearest kith and kin).
Shared decision making and proceedings of the committee should be documented
How a natural process of dying is facilitated?
Facilitating the natural process of dying without hastening or needless prolonging and providing active end of life care in a dying patient with a medically futile condition is called as Allowing Natural Death (AND).
How limitation of life sustaining treatment can take place in medically futile condition?
Once medically futile condition is agreed upon a team of clinicians and appropriate communication with family members has taken place, withholding a non-beneficial invasive complex medical intervention or phased withdrawal of the same in a dying patient (with medically futile condition) can be attempted.
Team of clinicians needs to ensure that the interventions are unlikely to confer any clinical benefit on the patient.
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for Quality Assurance in ICU
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_12NABH Standard No.:COP.09.g,d
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU

Quality Assurance:
It is an organized process that assesses and evaluates health services to improve practice or quality of care
Purpose:
To elaborate on the sequence of activities that are designed to implement the policies and procedures that are to be followed by the intensive care services.
To ensure that this program will achieve objectives of the above mentioned policy and ensure quality assurance for the intensive care services.
Objective:
To ensure that high standards of clinical practice are maintained through regular assessments.
The results of such assessments should be evaluated and acted on as necessary.
Responsibility:
Quality committee,
Clinical Audit committee
ICU doctors and intensivists
Quality Assurance Program:
The top management will ensure that adequate facilities are in place in the intensive care and high dependency units, to help providing high level of critical care for patients, in a right manner. This includes provision of correct environment, standardized equipments and instruments and employment of adequate and qualified support personnel.
The maintenance department will ensure that all engineering controls needed to prevent surgical site infection are in place.
The infection control team will carry out all necessary surveillance activities to ensure reduction and elimination of hospital acquired infections.
It will also monitor the housekeeping, laundry and sterilization activity to ensure correct procedures are followed.
Monitoring of Critical incidents and near misses and appropriate corrective and preventive actions
Risk management: actions to reduce risks to patients and staff in anaesthesia /critical care. A risk management programme undertakes identification of risks, assessment of risk factors, and control of risks.
The pharmacy committee will collaborate with intensivist and ensure that all necessary instruments and surgical consumables are made available for the surgeons used.
All staff should meticulously follow safe procedure guidelines to avoid wrong site, wrong side, wrong procedures.
The quality committee and the pharmacy committee will ensure that a suitable prophylactic and antibiotic policy is designed, documented, implemented and monitored. Based on outcome monitoring they will ensure corrective and preventive actions are instituted.
The infection control team will regularly monitor infection rates and inform to the infection control committee so that necessary preventive action can be taken.
The Intensivist in charge of ICU will regularly monitor for post-op complications including bleeding, re-intubation, ventilation, adverse drug reactions and the antibiotic administration and give feedback to the QMS team on a monthly basis. This data will be analyzed by the quality committee and corrective and preventive action initiated.
The quality committee and the clinical audit committee will ensure that only doctors who are educated, trained, registered and experienced to render intensive care services are allowed to do serve the patients in these settings.
The performance of all doctors in ICU will be continuously evaluated by these committees and action taken as and when needed.
Quality Parameters For Intensive Care Unit:
Quality of services in ICU means the quality of outcome of care provided. It means the level of proficiency in performing the designated functions and meeting the expectations of the clientele both external (patient / relatives) and internal (clinicians).
Expectation of the patient / relatives:
Patient with favourable prognosis and chances of recovery are nursed and treated back to recover from illness.
Intensive observation, monitoring & care to stop further deterioration of the condition.
Provision of specialized care and reversal of the patient’s condition.
Providing the level of care that can prevent any complications from occurring.
Expectation of the clinicians:
Continuous and complete monitoring of the patient condition so as to be alert and forewarned against any deterioration or unexpected changes in condition.
High quality nursing care to promote recovery and prevent deterioration. It means no bed sore, no falls, no nosocomial infections, no medication errors.
Timely & quick communication to the treating physician whenever there is a change in the condition warranting attention.
Equipment quality and availability:
Every bed must have piped gas and vacuum supply (1 oxygen outlet, 1 vacuum outlet), 5 electric sockets (including 1 multi electric socket) for using the equipments, nurse call bell buttons.
There should be bed side monitors, transport monitor, adequate number of infusion pumps, ventilators, USG equipment, ECG machine, defibrillator, suction machine and portable X-ray equipment, motorized /mechanically operated beds of right bed height with facility for sliding hard boards behind the patient’s back for resuscitation in the event of cardiac arrest.
Staffing:
The department should be under the charge of an Intensivist / Consultant trained in critical care.
The nurse: patient ratio may be between 1:1 (For venti.) and 1:2 (For non-venti.) during the day and evening shifts and between 1:2 (For venti.) and 1:3 (For non-venti.) during the night shift.
Quality of material, (drugs IV fluids, etc)
There should be a system of ensuring supply of stores (medical / non-medical) of quality and adequate quantity.
Engineering support services information and communication:
Temperature 20-250C, humidity 50-60%, 300 LUX diffuse light, uninterrupted stable power and adequate potable water supply should be ensured.
Quality Indicators captured in ICU: Refer above
Audit of quality assurance programs:
Quality assurance program will be reviewed extensively from time to time to ensure that remedial steps are taken wherever problems are identified and that subsequent review follows
Root cause analysis & RCA-CAPA
Policy Title:Policy and Procedure for counselling of patients & families ICU
Policy Code:HOSPITAL_ICU_13NABH Standard No.:COP.09.h
Policy Owner:ICU StaffDepartment:ICU

Aim:
To provide guidelines for counselling of patient & families.
Procedure:
Patients and families need to be counselled at periodic intervals (at-least once a day) by any doctor of the treating team to inform them and answer queries related to the changing condition of the patient.
The periodicity should be at least once a day or more often, based on the clinical condition of the patient and same needs to be documented.
Counselling of families of ICU patients is done in the designated counselling room.
